question: Which substance on red blood cells determines an individual's blood group?
explanation: Antigens located on the red blood cell membrane are the specific markers used to classify blood groups. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why do mismatched blood transfusions cause severe immune reactions?

options.A: Recipient red blood cells instantly dissolve
options.B: Hemoglobin turns into a toxic crystal
options.C: Donor plasma attacks recipient white cells
options.D: Donor antigens react with recipient antibodies

explanation: Natural antibodies in the recipient's plasma recognize foreign donor antigens and attack them, causing clumping or agglutination. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: What plasma antibodies are found in a patient with type AB blood?
explanation: Type AB blood contains both A and B antigens, so the body does not produce antibodies against them to prevent attacking its own cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why is type O blood considered the universal red cell donor?

options.A: It stimulates rapid white blood cell production.
options.B: It contains high levels of clotting factors.
options.C: Its plasma lacks all circulating antibodies.
options.D: Its red cells lack A and B antigens.

explanation: Because type O red blood cells carry no A or B antigens, the recipient's antibodies have nothing to attack. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which specific marker determines Rhesus compatibility?
explanation: The D antigen is the most important factor in determining whether blood is Rhesus positive or negative. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: How do Rhesus antibodies develop in an Rh-negative individual?

options.A: Through previous exposure to Rh-positive blood
options.B: Inherited naturally from parents at birth

explanation: Rh antibodies are not naturally present; they develop only after the immune system is exposed to Rh-positive red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of crossmatching blood before a transfusion?

options.A: Detecting adverse reactions between donor cells and recipient serum
options.B: Measuring the exact hemoglobin concentration of the donor bag
options.C: Screening the donated blood for viral infections like HIV
options.D: Determining the precise expiration date of the platelets

explanation: Crossmatching is the final safety check that mixes donor cells with recipient serum to ensure no reaction occurs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: What does reverse blood typing involve in the laboratory?

options.A: Centrifuging whole blood to separate plasma from platelets
options.B: Testing patient serum against known red blood cells
options.C: Mixing patient red cells with commercial anti-D serum
options.D: Heating the blood sample to destroy weak antibodies

explanation: Reverse typing checks the patient's serum against known red cells to confirm which antibodies are present. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which blood group is the universal recipient for packed red blood cells?
explanation: Type AB individuals lack both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in their plasma, so they will not attack incoming red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why is the compatibility rule reversed when transfusing only plasma instead of red blood cells?

options.A: Donated plasma is always filtered to remove cellular debris
options.B: Red blood cells lack the ability to carry clotting factors
options.C: Plasma proteins do not trigger immune responses in humans
options.D: Plasma contains antibodies rather than surface antigens

explanation: Plasma transfusions introduce antibodies into the recipient, so safety depends on ensuring those donor antibodies do not harm the recipient's cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a primary clinical sign of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
explanation: The breakdown of red blood cells releases free hemoglobin into the bloodstream, which passes into the urine and turns it dark. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)

question: When is anti-D immunoglobulin given to an Rh-negative pregnant woman to prevent sensitization?

options.A: Only after the infant is confirmed Rh-negative
options.B: After potential exposure to fetal blood
options.C: During the first trimester of every pregnancy
options.D: Immediately before starting routine iron therapy

explanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin clears any fetal Rh-positive cells before the mother's immune system can produce permanent antibodies against them. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)
